nameStory: Common flax gets its name from the Old English 'fleax,' meaning 'to plait' or weave, referring to its ancient use in making linen cloth. The scientific name 'usitatissimum' literally means 'most useful,' which perfectly captures how valuable this plant has been to humans for thousands of years. It's also called linseed when people are talking about its oil-rich seeds.
description: Common flax is a slender annual plant that grows 2-4 feet tall with delicate blue flowers and narrow leaves. This graceful plant has been cultivated for so long that it's only known from gardens and farms - you won't find it growing wild anywhere in the world. Its stems are remarkably strong and fibrous, which is exactly what makes it perfect for spinning into linen thread. While not native to New England, you might spot it growing in herb gardens or small farm plots where people are experimenting with traditional fiber crops.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five delicate sky-blue petals that feel papery thin and drop off easily when touched. Each flower is about the size of a dime and opens fresh each morning, lasting just one day.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel smooth and slightly waxy, arranged alternately up the stem like tiny green ribbons. They're typically 1-2 inches long and point upward.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in a neat, upright clump with multiple slender stems that sway gracefully in the breeze. The whole plant has an airy, delicate appearance despite its surprisingly tough stems.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round seed capsules about the size of a small pea that rattle when shaken, containing glossy brown seeds that feel smooth and slippery when rubbed between your fingers.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Remarkably strong and fibrous stems that are difficult to break by hand, with a smooth surface that feels almost silky when you run your fingers along it.

habitat: In New England, you'll find common flax only where people have planted it - in herb gardens, historical farm demonstrations, or small experimental fiber plots. It prefers full sun and well-drained soil, and won't survive New England winters since it's an annual that must be replanted each year. Look for it at living history museums or farms that focus on traditional crafts and heritage crops.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted after the last frost, and young seedlings emerge looking like tiny grass with their narrow leaves. The plants grow rapidly in the lengthening days.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with fresh blue flowers opening each morning from June through August. This is when the plant is most recognizable and beautiful.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and round seed capsules develop, turning brown and rattling in the wind. The whole plant begins to turn golden as it prepares to die back.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence since it's an annual, though some seeds may overwinter in the soil to potentially sprout the following spring.

funFact: The ancient Egyptians wrapped their mummies in linen made from flax, and some of those 4,000-year-old bandages are still intact today - proving that flax fiber is incredibly durable and long-lasting!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other blue wildflowers, but flax's combination of papery five-petaled flowers, extremely narrow leaves, and tall slender growth habit is quite distinctive. The key memory trick: if it looks delicate but the stem won't break easily in your hands, it's probably flax.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with New Zealand flax, which is a completely different plant in the genus Phormium. Common flax is the source of both linen fabric (from the stems) and linseed oil (from the seeds) - it's literally the same plant serving two very different purposes depending on which part you use.
compareHints: Common flax stands out from its wild New England relatives by being much taller and more robust than species like Fairy Flax, and having blue flowers instead of the yellow blooms found on Ridged Yellow Flax or Stiff Yellow Flax. Its cultivated nature also means it grows in neat patches rather than scattered wild populations, and its stems are much more fibrous and strong than any of the wild flax species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sandplain Flax differs from other New England flax species primarily by its habitat preference for sandy soils and coastal areas.

Ridged Yellow Flax stands out from its New England flax relatives primarily by those distinctive stem ridges - Stiff Yellow Flax has smooth stems and grows more upright, while Virginia Flax has smooth stems and much smaller white or pale yellow flowers.
Among New England's flax species, scarlet flax is the only one with bright red flowers - all our native flaxes have yellow, blue, or white blooms.

Virginia Flax is distinguished from other wild flaxes in New England by its yellow flowers and branching habit - Fairy Flax has white flowers, while the yellow-flowered Ridged Yellow Flax has more linear leaves and grows in different habitats.
Fairy flax stands out from other New England flax species by being much smaller and more delicate than its relatives.
Perennial flax stands out from other New England flax species by its perennial nature and pure blue flowers.
Among the yellow-flowered flax species in eastern North America, Stiff Yellow Flax stands out for its notably rigid stems that won't bend easily.
